newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers attack beef crisis plans.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers attack beef crisis plans.

text.p: European farm ministers attacked proposals on Monday to pay grain farmers less so beef farmers can get more to help them cope with the mad cow crisis.

Several hundred German farmers demonstrated behind barbed wire barriers outside the ministerial building, chanting "Fischler out" and "Fischler the executioner of German farmers", a reference to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
"The proposals are ineffective and make certain regions in Europe pay for others," German Secretary of State for Agriculture, Franz-Josef Feiter, told reporters.
"The (farmers') situation is extremely difficult. I would call it explosive," he added.
Germany, backed by most EU member states, argues that cereals farmers, who have been reaping bumper profits from record world prices, could soon be confronted with falling prices as production rises.

Feiter said that savings could be made within the farm budget to find the 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.7 billion) needed in 1998 to ease the problems caused by the crisis over the disease, properly called Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
The European Commission flatly rejected this.
But the Commission's agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said that there wrere many problems over its proposals to curb a growing mountain of surplus beef caused by a fall in demand.
"There's no major concensus over what should be done," Kiely told reporters after the first day of the two-day meeting.
Earlier, British Farm Minister Douglas Hogg met Fischler to press the case for cutting a scheme to slaughter an extra 147,000 cattle in Britain most at risk of developing BSE.
The scheme was part of a package agreed by EU heads of state at their summit in Florence, Italy, in June aimed at gradually lifting a ban on British beef exports.
A report by Oxford University scientists published by Nature magazine last month said BSE would disappear within five years even without an extra cull.
"It is clearly right that we should talk with member states about the impact of all this information," Hogg told a briefing.
Hogg said he would also tell ministers on Tuesday of British progress in implementing the Florence agreement.
Britain has already culled around 500,000 older cattle over 30 months old under a separate scheme, introduced a cattle passport system, tightened animal feed and abattoir controls.
Hogg added that Britain would also have to make its own judgement of the likelihood of member states "rapidly and substantially" lifting the ban if a cull was implemented.
"There are some actions of some member states which are difficult to reconcile with previous decisions," Hogg said.
EU officials noted that another recent British study found that mad cow disease could be passed from cow to calf, implying that more animals would have to be slaughtered.
But Hogg said that it could mean that cows were merely passing on a "susceptibility to contaminated feedstuffs" which had now been removed from the food chain.
Ministers offered little short-term prospect of either reducing the British cattle cull or easing the export ban.
"The Florence agreement is the only way to lift the embargo. Any other way would exacerbate tension," said Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, whose country has the EU presidency.
"As long as it's uncertain there is no BSE risk from Britain, there can't be any lifting of the ban," Germany's Feiter said.
